Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative primarily unfolds as a real-time scene, grounded in immediate sensory details (the smell of diesel and wet wood, the sound of the ferry against the dock), dialogue, and physical actions (Ilse coiling the rope, Jonas pulling his suitcase). Rather than interrupting the pacing with long blocks of exposition, the writer seamlessly weaves brief moments of summary and backstory directly into the characters' present observations—such as the mention of how Jonas used to look arriving from the train, the wrench and jacket belonging to the late Henning, and the childhood mug at the back of the cabinet. This approach keeps the reader engaged in the immediate tension between mother and son while effortlessly providing the necessary emotional and historical context.
